raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 21-year-old girl experienced 1 week of significant dysuria and weariness, with the subsequent development of blurry vision, slight dysphagia, slurred speech, and sensory disturbance. Her past medical history and family history were both unremarkable. Routine laboratory investigations revealed that complete blood count, liver and renal tests, tumor markers, rheumatoid factors, folic acid, and vitamin B12 were normal. Antithyroglobulin antibody (33.3 IU/ml; normal range: 0-4 IU/ml) and antithyroid peroxidase antibody (28.0 IU/ml; normal range: 0-9 IU/ml) were positive in the serum. Antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and syphilis were negative. Electrocardiogram, chest X-ray, abdominal ultrasonography, and gynecological ultrasonography were normal.
Lumbar puncture revealed a high white blood cell count (24/mm3) with 70% monocytes and an elevated protein level of 0.59 g/l (normal range: 0.15-0.45 g/l). Human cytomegalovirus IgG and rubella virus IgG antibodies were positive. CSF levels of IgA, IgG, and IgM were 6.42 mg/l, 62.2 mg/l (normal range: 0-34 mg/l), and 1.53 mg/l, respectively, and the IgG index was 1.21. Viral, fungal, and bacterial polymerase chain reaction (PCR), cultures, and cytology were negative and no malignant cells were found in the CSF.
Cervical spinal cord MRI showed diffuse cord edema. A clinical diagnosis of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders was originally considered and thus this patient received intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg per day for five consecutive days with minimal improvement. Using transfected cell-based immunofluorescence assays, we detected GFAP-IgG in the CSF (Figure 1a) and aquaporin 4 (AQP4)-IgG in serum (Figure 1b). GFAP and AQP4 antibodies in the CSF and serum were assessed by an immunofluorescence assay using rat hippocampus tissue, and by a cell-based assay using HEK293 cells transfected with GFAP and AQP4, as reported previously. Both tests were repeated the following day using the new experimental materials and the same equipment to confirm the positive findings when positive results were first detected. Tests of other autoantibodies in CSF and serum, including MOG-IgG, MBP-IgG, AQP1-IgG, NMDAR-IgG, AMPA1-IgG, AMPA2-IgG, LGI1-IgG, CASPR2-IgG, and GABABR-IgG, were negative. As GFAP-IgG was reported to be a specific biomarker of autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy and CSF is more reliable than serum for GFAP-IgG testing, other similar diseases were additionally and carefully ruled out and the diagnosis of autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy was confirmed.
Thorough brain and spinal cord MRI examinations were performed. Interestingly, spinal cord MRIs showed longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions involving the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal cord in T2-weighted images, with spinal cord central canal, patchy, punctate, and pia enhancement lesions extending up to the medulla oblongata in T1-weighted images (Figure 2). Surprisingly, MRI scans of the cerebral hemisphere, midbrain, pons, and cerebellar were normal. The most common characteristic of autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy (linear, radial perivascular patterns of enhancement throughout the cerebral white matter) was not found in this patient (Figure 2a).
Given her symptoms and MRI results, the diagnosis of autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy was finally considered. The patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg for 4 days) followed by a 50% reduction of the dose after 3-5 days, and subsequent oral methylprednisolone (60 mg/day), which was then tapered (reduced 4 mg/day every 2 weeks). Owing to the potential possibility of relapse, she received mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily. Four weeks after discharge, the patient's neurological symptoms had significantly improved.
During the follow-up period, the patient reported mild sensory abnormality and was independent in all activities of daily living 3 months after the diagnosis of GFAP astrocytopathy. Repeated MRI scans were performed, showing residual T2 hyperintensities and T1-gadolinium enhancement in the spinal cord and medulla oblongata with no evidence of new lesions (Figure 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old previously healthy woman presented with a 1-week history of significant dysuria and fatigue, followed by blurred vision, mild dysphagia, slurred speech, and sensory disturbances.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy, the patient experienced 1 week of urinary dysuria and fatigue before developing progressive neurological symptoms including blurred vision, mild dysphagia, dysarthria, and sensory disturbance.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical and family history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1 week of dysuria and weariness/fatigue, followed by blurred vision, slight dysphagia, slurred speech, and sensory disturbance.

objective.physical_examination: Bulbar and sensory neurological deficits (blurred vision, mild dysphagia, slurred speech, and sensory disturbance).
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, liver and renal function tests, tumor markers, rheumatoid factor, folic acid, and vitamin B12 were normal. Serum anti-thyroglobulin antibody (33.3 IU/mL; normal 0-4 IU/mL) and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody (28.0 IU/mL; normal 0-9 IU/mL) were elevated. Serum ANA, ANCA, HIV, HBV, HCV, and syphilis were negative; serum human cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG and rubella virus IgG were positive. ECG, chest X-ray, abdominal ultrasound, and gynecological ultrasound were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture revealed CSF pleocytosis (WBC 24/mm3, 70% monocytes), elevated protein 0.59 g/L (normal 0.15-0.45 g/L), CSF IgA 6.42 mg/L, elevated CSF IgG 62.2 mg/L (normal 0-34 mg/L), CSF IgM 1.53 mg/L, elevated IgG index 1.21, and negative CSF viral/fungal/bacterial PCRs, cultures, and cytology. Cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal cord MRI demonstrated longitudinally extensive T2-weighted spinal cord lesions and cord edema with central canal, patchy, punctate, and pial T1 gadolinium enhancement extending superiorly to the medulla oblongata (brain, midbrain, pons, and cerebellar MRI were normal without radial perivascular enhancement). Cell-based and rat hippocampus tissue immunofluorescence assays detected glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)-IgG in the CSF and aquaporin-4 (AQP4)-IgG in the serum (negative for MOG, MBP, AQP1, NMDAR, AMPA1/2, LGI1, CASPR2, and GABABR antibodies).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of autoimmune glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) astrocytopathy with coexisting serum AQP4-IgG presenting as longitudinally extensive encephalomyelitis involving the medulla oblongata and entire spinal cord (confirmed by positive CSF GFAP-IgG and serum AQP4-IgG on repeated cell-based and tissue immunofluorescence assays, with CNS viral/bacterial/fungal infections ruled out). After minimal response to a 5-day course of IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day), treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg/day for 4 days, halved after 3-5 days, then oral methylprednisolone 60 mg/day tapered by 4 mg/day every 2 weeks) and maintenance mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg twice daily) resulted in marked neurological improvement at 4 weeks and full ADL independence with only mild residual sensory symptoms at 3-month follow-up.
